title: And besides · looks like
titleJp: おいしそうだし、安いし
canDo: I can give two or more reasons in a single sentence with 〜し〜し and put the conclusion at the end: この店は安いし、料理もおいしいし、よく来ます。
I can build 〜し with the right short form for each kind of word, without forgetting the だ of nouns and な-adjectives: 日曜日だし, しずかだし.
I can say how something looks, from what I see, with 〜そうです: おいしそう, たいへんそう, 元気そう, and the irregular よさそう and なさそう.
I can warn that something looks like it is about to happen with verb stem + そう: 雨がふりそうです。
I can tell the appearance そう of this lesson apart from the hearsay そうです ("I heard that…"), which comes in Lesson 17: おいしそうです × おいしいそうです.

blocks.t: Warm-up: say out loud the short forms (affirmative and negative, present and past) of 2 verbs, 2 い-adjectives, 2 な-adjectives and 2 nouns (lessons 08-1 and 09-1)
Vocabulary: tap 🔊 on each word and repeat it twice
Grammar: the 2 points, each with its examples read aloud and one 🔬
Video (block 6), only the parts on 〜し and 〜そう
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key
Checklist (block 10) + write your questions in the lesson notebook

skills: Short forms of verbs, adjectives and nouns, in the present and the past (lessons 08-1 and 09-1). 〜し is built straight from them.
Giving a reason with 〜から and 〜ので (lessons 06-4, 09-3 and 12-2). 〜し is the way to give more than one.
The ます stem, that is, the ます form without ます (行き, 食べ, ふり), which you used in 〜に行く (lesson 07-3) and 〜たい (lesson 11-1). It is the base of 〜そう with verbs.
い- and な-adjectives, and the irregular negative いい → よくない (lesson 05-1).

vocab.en: and besides, and what's more (links reasons; comes after the short form)
looks…, seems… (from appearance, from what you see)
near, close (駅から近い = close to the station)
to fall (rain, snow): 雨がふる = to rain
to fall, drop (from a high place): コップがおちる
to quit, stop (a job, a habit)
to get tired (つかれている = to be tired)

grammar.title: 〜し〜し: stacking reasons
grammar.explanation:
〜し is for **stacking reasons**: "it's cheap, and besides, the food is good, so…". You list two reasons (or more), each ending in **し**, and the **conclusion** comes at the end. し carries a sense of "and there's more": it suggests these are not the only reasons.
• **Form**: short form + し. It is the same short form as in lessons 08-1 and 09-1.
• Verbs: ある → あるし; ない → ないし; 行った → 行ったし.
• い-adjectives: 安い → 安いし; 安くない → 安くないし; いい → いいし.
• な-adjectives and nouns: in the present affirmative, **だ** comes in. しずかだし; 日曜日だし. In the other forms, it is the normal short form: しずかじゃないし; 休みだったし.
• **The conclusion goes at the end**, and it decides whether the sentence is polite: 安いし、おいしいし、よく来ます。 The reasons with し stay in the short form even in a sentence with ます. In very formal conversation you will also hear ですし and ますし.
• In English you can put the conclusion first ("I come here often because…"). In Japanese, the reasons come first and the conclusion always comes last.
• The conclusion can be **left unsaid**. When turning something down, it is common to stop after the reasons: あしたはテストがあるし、お金もないし… and the other person understands the "no". It is the same spirit as the ちょっと… of lesson 03-3.
• **も** is very common in the reasons: 料理**も**おいしいし ("the food is good, too"). も reinforces the idea of "one more reason".
• **し × から**: から gives **the** reason, directly. し stacks reasons and hints that there are others. Even a single reason with し (時間もないし…) sounds like "among other things".
• In the sentence, each block with し is a **reason**, and the **PREDICATE** is the conclusion, at the end. Read from the end: "I come here often" → why? → it's cheap, and the food is good too.
grammar.structure: [reason 1 in short form] し、[reason 2] し、[conclusion]。 · noun / な-adj. + だし

examples.jp: この店は安いし、料理もおいしいし、よく来ます。
examples.kana: このみせはやすいし、りょうりもおいしいし、よくきます。
examples.romaji: Kono mise wa yasui shi, ryōri mo oishii shi, yoku kimasu.
examples.en: This restaurant is cheap, and the food is good too, so I come here often.

examples.jp: 今日は日曜日だし、天気がいいし、海に行きましょう。
examples.kana: きょうはにちようびだし、てんきがいいし、うみにいきましょう。
examples.romaji: Kyō wa nichiyōbi da shi, tenki ga ii shi, umi ni ikimashō.
examples.en: It's Sunday today, and the weather is nice, so let's go to the beach!

examples.jp: 今日、飲みに行かない？— うーん、あしたはテストがあるし、お金もないし…
examples.kana: きょう、のみにいかない？— うーん、あしたはテストがあるし、おかねもないし…
examples.romaji: Kyō, nomi ni ikanai? — Ūn, ashita wa tesuto ga aru shi, okane mo nai shi…
examples.en: Want to go out for a drink today? — Hmm, I have a test tomorrow, and I don't have any money either…

pitfalls: Nouns and な-adjectives need だ: しずかし ✗ → しずかだし ✓; 日曜日し ✗ → 日曜日だし ✓.
い-adjectives don't take だ: 安いだし ✗ → 安いし ✓.
Before し comes a complete form that could end a sentence on its own, never the ます stem: 行きし ✗ → 行くし ✓ (or 行きますし, very formal).
し links whole clauses (reasons, qualities), not bare nouns the way English "and" does. "Bread and milk" is still パンとぎゅうにゅう (lesson 04-3): パンしぎゅうにゅう ✗.
howToStudy: Think of something you like (a place, a food, a game) and say out loud 3 sentences with two reasons each: 〜し、〜し、好きです。 At least one reason should be a noun or a な-adjective + だし.

Tap 🔬 on example 2. Each reason (日曜日だし, いいし) becomes its own block before the PREDICATE 行きましょう, which is the conclusion, an invitation. 🔬 doesn't have a label for し yet and marks those blocks as NO PARTICLE: read them as REASONS. Notice that 天気が is the SUBJECT of いいし.
Turn down 3 imaginary invitations out loud, the Japanese way, giving only the reasons and never saying "no": あしたは仕事があるし、ちょっとつかれているし…

grammar.title: 〜そうです: looks like (appearance)
grammar.gloss: おいしそう, よさそう, 雨がふりそう
grammar.explanation:
〜そうです says how something **looks**, from what you see (or sense) right now: "looks delicious", "looks tough", "looks like it's going to rain". It is a **guess from appearance**, before you confirm. Once you have tasted the cake, you no longer say おいしそう: you say おいしい！
• **い-adjectives**: drop い and add そう. おいし|い → おいしそう; ねむい → ねむそう; からい → からそう.
• **な-adjectives**: the word + そう, without な. 元気そう; たいへんそう; ひまそう; べんりそう.
• **Two irregulars**: **いい → よさそう** and **ない → なさそう**. This also applies when ない ends a phrase: 時間がない → 時間がなさそう.
• **Negative** adjectives: おいしくない → おいしくなさそう (doesn't look tasty); ひまじゃない → ひまじゃなさそう.
• **Verbs**: ます stem + そう = "looks like it's going to…", a prediction from what you see. ふります → **ふりそう** (雨がふりそう: the sky is dark); おちます → **おちそう** (the thing is right on the edge).
• **Other people's feelings**: you can't feel what someone else feels, so you describe it from their face: うれしそう (looks happy), さびしそう (looks sad, lonely), ねむそう… This is very common.
• 〜そう **behaves like a な-adjective**: おいしそう**です** at the end of a sentence; おいしそう**な**ケーキ before a noun; おいしそう**に**食べる (eats with obvious enjoyment). In the past: おいしそうでした (it looked delicious).
• In the sentence, [word + そう] + です is the **PREDICATE**. With な, it becomes a block that DESCRIBES NEXT: やさしそうな | 人.

**Careful: this is not the hearsay そうです.** Genki Lesson 17 (lesson 17-1 of this course) brings another そうです, which means "**I heard that…**" and comes after the **complete short form**: おいしいそうです = "I heard it's delicious" (someone told me). Here, the word is **cut**: おいしそうです = "it looks delicious" (I can see it). One extra い changes everything. The same goes for な: 元気そうです (looks well) × 元気だそうです (I heard they're well).
grammar.structure: [い-adj. minus い] そう · [な-adj.] そう · いい → よさそう · ない → なさそう · [verb stem] そう · 〜そうな + N

examples.jp: わあ、このケーキ、おいしそう！
examples.kana: わあ、このケーキ、おいしそう！

examples.jp: 新しい店長はやさしそうな人ですね。— ええ、ほんとうにやさしいですよ。
examples.kana: あたらしいてんちょうはやさしそうなひとですね。— ええ、ほんとうにやさしいですよ。
examples.romaji: Atarashii tenchō wa yasashisō na hito desu ne. — Ē, hontō ni yasashii desu yo.
examples.en: The new manager seems like a kind person, right? — Yes, they really are kind.

examples.jp: あ、雨がふりそうですね。かさを持って行きましょう。
examples.kana: あ、あめがふりそうですね。かさをもっていきましょう。
examples.romaji: A, ame ga furisō desu ne. Kasa o motte ikimashō.
examples.en: Oh, it looks like it's going to rain. Let's take umbrellas.

pitfalls: Don't confuse it with the hearsay of lesson 17-1: おいしそうです = it looks delicious (I can see it) × おいしいそうです = I heard it's delicious (someone told me). For "looks", the word is cut: おいしいそう ✗ → おいしそう ✓.
いい and ない are irregular: いそう ✗ → よさそう ✓; なそう ✗ → なさそう ✓ (時間がなさそう).

かわいそう does not mean "looks cute": it is a different word, "poor thing, what a pity". For something you can see is cute, say かわいい！ ✓. With qualities that are obvious at a glance (きれい, colors), そう is generally not used: looking at the flower in front of you, きれいそうですね ✗ → きれいですね ✓.
English says "looks like a student" with the same word "look", but そう doesn't attach to nouns: 学生そう ✗. For "seems to be a student" there is 〜みたい, which comes in lesson 17-3: 学生みたい ✓.
howToStudy: Make a table in your notebook with 10 words (4 い-adjectives, 3 な-adjectives, いい, ない and 2 verbs) and write the そう form next to each one. Read it aloud and highlight よさそう and なさそう in color.
Tap 🔬 on example 2. やさしそうな shows up as DESCRIBES NEXT, attached to 人, and 人ですね is the PREDICATE. In the answer, the PREDICATE やさしいですよ has no そう: now it is a certainty, not a guess.
Open photos on your phone (food, places, people) and comment on each one out loud with そう: おいしそう！, 高そう…, ねむそう… When you see a gray sky, say 雨がふりそうですね。
grammar.flag: Check whether your Genki II also covers そう with verbs (ふりそう, おちそう) in this point. It is the same そう and standard grammar; if your book only presents the adjectives in this lesson, treat the verb part as a bonus.

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook. Write the kanji you already know and the rest in kana. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it the next day. If you have the Genki II Workbook, do this lesson's exercises too.

tasks.prompt: Say how it looks, with 〜そうです. Before writing, check the kind of word: い-adjective, な-adjective, verb, or one of the irregulars.

items.note: い-adjective: drop い and add そう.
な-adjective: the word + そう, without な.
Irregular: いい → よさそう.

a.kana: じかんがなさそうです

items.note: Irregular: ない → なさそう.
Verb: ます stem (ふります → ふり) + そう = it looks like it's going to rain.
Looks well. Don't confuse it with 元気だそうです, "I heard they're well" (hearsay, lesson 17-1).

tasks.prompt: Join the two reasons with 〜し and write the whole sentence, with the conclusion at the end. Use も in the second reason when it sounds natural.

items.q: 駅から近い ＋ へやが広い → このアパートがいいです。

a.jp: 駅から近いし、へやも広いし、このアパートがいいです。
a.kana: えきからちかいし、へやもひろいし、このアパートがいいです。
a.romaji: Eki kara chikai shi, heya mo hiroi shi, kono apāto ga ii desu.

items.note: い-adjective: straight + し. へやが広い is also correct; も reinforces "one more reason".

items.q: 今日は休み (noun) ＋ 天気がいい → こうえんに行きませんか。

a.jp: 今日は休みだし、天気もいいし、こうえんに行きませんか。
a.kana: きょうはやすみだし、てんきもいいし、こうえんにいきませんか。
a.romaji: Kyō wa yasumi da shi, tenki mo ii shi, kōen ni ikimasen ka.

items.note: 休み is a noun: 休みだし.

items.q: 田中さん: 親切（な） ＋ おもしろい → みんなに人気があります。

a.jp: 田中さんは親切だし、おもしろいし、みんなに人気があります。
a.kana: たなかさんはしんせつだし、おもしろいし、みんなににんきがあります。
a.romaji: Tanaka-san wa shinsetsu da shi, omoshiroi shi, minna ni ninki ga arimasu.

items.note: 親切 is a な-adjective: 親切だし. Here し lists qualities that explain the popularity.

items.q: (turning down an invitation) きのうあまりねなかった ＋ あたまがいたい → 今日は…

a.jp: きのうあまりねなかったし、あたまもいたいし、今日は…
a.kana: きのうあまりねなかったし、あたまもいたいし、きょうは…
a.romaji: Kinō amari nenakatta shi, atama mo itai shi, kyō wa…

items.note: Past negative in the short form: ねなかったし. The conclusion is left unsaid: it is a polite refusal.

items.q: この仕事: きゅうりょうがよくない ＋ たいへん（な） → やめたいです。

a.jp: この仕事はきゅうりょうもよくないし、たいへんだし、やめたいです。
a.kana: このしごとはきゅうりょうもよくないし、たいへんだし、やめたいです。
a.romaji: Kono shigoto wa kyūryō mo yokunai shi, taihen da shi, yametai desu.

items.note: The negative of いい: よくないし. たいへん is a な-adjective: たいへんだし.

tasks.prompt: Translate into Japanese. In the sentences with "looks", use 〜そう.

a.jp: このカレーはからそうです。
マリアさんは今日、ねむそうです。
a.kana: マリアさんはきょう、ねむそうです。

items.note: Another person's feeling or state: describe it from their appearance, with そう.

a.jp: この店は高くなさそうです。
a.kana: このみせはたかくなさそうです。

items.note: Negative: 高くない → 高くなさそう.

items.q: I bought a bag that looked handy.

a.jp: べんりそうなかばんを買いました。
a.kana: べんりそうなかばんをかいました。

items.q: Oh, this glass looks like it's going to fall!

a.jp: あ、このコップ、おちそうですよ。
a.romaji: A, kono koppu, ochisō desu yo.

items.note: The verb おちる: stem おち + そう.

items.q: I'm not going today: I'm tired, and I have work tomorrow too.

a.jp: 今日はつかれているし、あしたも仕事があるし、行きません。
a.kana: きょうはつかれているし、あしたもしごとがあるし、いきません。
a.romaji: Kyō wa tsukarete iru shi, ashita mo shigoto ga aru shi, ikimasen.

items.note: In Japanese the reasons come first and the conclusion goes at the end: the opposite order of this English sentence.

tasks.prompt: Show a Japanese friend a photo of a place you recommend (a restaurant, a bakery, a square). Write 4 or 5 sentences: 1 with two reasons in 〜し〜し, 1 with 〜そうな + noun, 1 with adjective + そうです and 1 with verb + そう. Then read them aloud and record yourself on your phone.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: この店は駅から近いし、安いし、よく行きます。写真を見てください。おいしそうなパンがたくさんありますね。店長もやさしそうです。でも、いつも人が多くて、パンがすぐなくなりそうです。
a.kana: このみせはえきからちかいし、やすいし、よくいきます。しゃしんをみてください。おいしそうなパンがたくさんありますね。てんちょうもやさしそうです。でも、いつもひとがおおくて、パンがすぐなくなりそうです。
a.romaji: Kono mise wa eki kara chikai shi, yasui shi, yoku ikimasu. Shashin o mite kudasai. Oishisō na pan ga takusan arimasu ne. Tenchō mo yasashisō desu. Demo, itsumo hito ga ōkute, pan ga sugu nakunarisō desu.
a.en: This shop is close to the station and it's cheap, so I go there often. Look at the photo. There's lots of delicious-looking bread, isn't there? The manager looks kind, too. But it's always crowded, and it looks like the bread is going to run out soon.

items.note: Check: the reasons with し in the short form and the conclusion at the end; そうな before a noun; the い-adjective without its い before そう; and the verb in the stem form (なくなります → なくなり) + そう.

practice.what: Play normally, ideally in an N4-level area if you have reached one. Hunt the dialogues for two kinds of sentences: reasons with 〜し and comments with 〜そう. When you find a そう, say out loud the word it came from (つよそう → つよい). Log the session in Immersion → Games and paste one of those lines into 🔬 Anatomy.

Drills → Conjugation: warm up the short forms (present and past, affirmative and negative), the base of 〜し. Then Drills → 🔬 Anatomy → 🧱 Build from the end with example 1 of point a, starting from 来ます.

Write 3 sentences in the Journal: one with 〜し〜し about why you study Japanese and two with 〜そう about things or people you saw today. Open "Anatomy of what I wrote" and check that the conclusion ended up as the PREDICATE, at the end.
Tap 🔊 on each example in this lesson and repeat along 3 times. In おいしそう, the そう is long: お・い・し・そ・う is 5 equal beats. Don't shorten it to 4.
Record your recommendation from homework h4 in 40 seconds or less, as if you were showing the photo to a friend. Listen and check that each そう came out with the word cut (おいしそう, not おいしいそう).

culture.title: ゆるキャラ: mascots
culture.body: In Japan, many cities, prefectures, companies and even public bodies such as the police have a **mascot**. The cute, slightly clumsy ones are called **ゆるキャラ**: ゆるい ("loose, relaxed") + キャラ ("character"). They promote tourism, local products and campaigns, and they usually appear at events, on posters and packaging and in souvenir shops, often with their own name and their own social media profile. One of the best known is **くまモン**, a black bear with red cheeks from Kumamoto Prefecture, who appears on products all over the country. For several years there was even a national contest decided by public vote, the ゆるキャラグランプリ. In front of a mascot, you will often hear comments with this lesson's そう: やさしそう, ねむそう, 元気そう…
culture.try: Look up a photo of a ゆるキャラ (くまモン, for example) and describe it out loud in 3 sentences with そう: やさしそうです。… Then invent a mascot for your city and say why it is good, with 〜し〜し: かわいいし、元気だし、みんなに人気がありそうです。

checklist: I can give two reasons in one sentence with 〜し〜し, without looking, and put the conclusion at the end.
I remember the だ with nouns and な-adjectives (日曜日だし, しずかだし), and I know that い-adjectives don't take だ.
I can say how something looks with 〜そうです (おいしそう, たいへんそう, 元気そう) and use 〜そうな before a noun.
I use the irregulars without thinking: いい → よさそう, ない → なさそう.
I use verb stem + そう for "looks like it's going to…": 雨がふりそうです。
I know that おいしそうです (it looks delicious) and おいしいそうです (I heard it's delicious, Lesson 17) are different things.
I did the homework, checked it against the answer key and redid what I got wrong.
If I have the Genki II Workbook: I did the 〜し and 〜そうです exercises.
